rule: decision 47: a mapping the blind verifier did not confirm is held — never shown, never a diagnosis, never S5 evidence — until a human keeps or drops it

items.stem: A $\text{25}$ $\text{m}$ ladder rests against a vertical wall with its foot $\text{15}$ $\text{m}$ from the wall. Build a right triangle, of any size, whose marked angle $\theta$ equals the angle between the ladder and the wall.
items.construction: The ladder is the hypotenuse (25 m) and the 15 m foot-to-wall distance is the side opposite the angle between ladder and wall (the angle at the top of the ladder). The wall height is 20 m by Pythagoras. So sin theta = 15/25 = 0.6 (cos 0.8, tan 0.75). On the instrument, drag the leg opposite the marked angle theta to 3 and the leg adjacent to theta to 4. The hypotenuse is then 5 and sin = 3/5 = 0.6. Opposite 6 and adjacent 8, or opposite 15 and adjacent 20, also work because grading is on the ratio. The target is above 0 and below 1, so every limit is satisfied.
items.predicate_meaning: Built the tangent where another ratio was asked for
items.misconception_label: Writes sine as opposite over adjacent
items.misconception_description: The student finds the opposite and adjacent sides correctly but writes sine as the opposite side over the adjacent side, which is the tangent's pair of sides, so no hypotenuse appears in the answer.
items.why: This predicate fires when tan of the built angle is 0.6, for example opposite 3 and adjacent 5. A student who writes sine as opposite over adjacent and finds the sides correctly would take opposite 15 and adjacent 20, and tan = 0.75. That is the correct 3-4-5 triangle, with sin 0.6, so it would be graded correct and would not fire. The tan = 0.6 build mostly comes from a different slip: using the ladder length 25 as a leg beside the 15 foot distance. That is a hypotenuse-versus-leg error, not sine-as-opposite-over-adjacent, so the diagnosis would refute a mistake the student did not make.

items.stem: From the top of a $\text{30}$ $\text{m}$ cliff, a boat on the level sea is seen at an angle of depression $\theta$. The boat is $\text{40}$ $\text{m}$ from the foot of the cliff. Build a right triangle, of any size, whose marked angle $\theta$ equals this angle of depression.
items.construction: The angle of depression is measured down from the horizontal at the cliff top, so by alternate angles it equals the angle of elevation at the boat. In the right triangle (cliff vertical, sea level horizontal, right angle at the foot of the cliff) that angle sits at the boat. The side opposite it is the cliff, 30 m. The side adjacent to it is the 40 m distance along the sea. So tan θ = 30/40 = 0.75. The question gives only the two legs, so tan is the ratio asked for. On the instrument I put the marked angle θ at the end of the horizontal leg, set the horizontal leg to 4 and the vertical leg to 3 (or 8 and 6, or 40 and 30 if the scale allows), and the live readout shows tan = 0.75. Sin reads 0.6 and cos reads 0.8, which is consistent. Every similar triangle is accepted.
items.predicate_meaning: Built the sine where another ratio was asked for
items.misconception_label: Choosing the hypotenuse from the angle θ, not from the right angle
items.misconception_description: The student picks as the hypotenuse a side that forms $\theta$ or faces $\theta$, instead of the side directly opposite the right angle, so the true hypotenuse ends up called adjacent or opposite.
items.why: used-sine is listed for tan, so it can fire. It fires when the student builds sin = 0.75 (hypotenuse 4, leg 3, tan about 1.13) in place of tan = 0.75. The claimed cause is calling a side that forms θ the hypotenuse. Here the cliff and the sea are plainly perpendicular and the two given lengths are the legs, so a student has little reason to treat 40 as the hypotenuse. A sin = 0.75 build here would mostly come from reaching for the wrong ratio (confusing SOH with TOA, or reading 30/40 as 'opposite over the longer side'). It would not come from misidentifying the hypotenuse, so the diagnosis would mostly be wrong.
